[quote=dhornaper;61267062][Spoiler=[b][U]Il-76 Special Delivery[/u][/b]]

The hum of the engines was heard long before the aircraft was seen. The Dhora Il-76 broke through the morning mist and touched down with a thunderous thud. In the next hour, all three Il-76s would land in a Tirakan airbase, all painted in the same signature grey.

The Dhora officers directed the Tirakan servicemen as they offloaded its cargo. The first plane carried four P-18-2 early warning radars, digital solid-state versions of the faithful P-18 that had served Dhora SAM teams well across decades. The second had an endless array of crates. Spare parts for the newly delivered P‑18s and Pantsirs. The third carried pallets of ammunition: missiles sealed in protective canisters and belts of autocannon rounds.

Alongside the equipment was a delegation of Dhora officers. These were veterans, SAM teams that had operated their equipment for at least a decade, and here to train Tirakan's officers in operating the Pantsirs and P-18s.[/spoiler]

[Spoiler=[b][u]Training[/u][/b]]

Colonel Hussein and his lieutenants stand in front of the assembled Tirakan SAM teams. Around them are the P-18 radars and Pantsirs he's there to train them to become proficient in.

"Soldiers, we, as SAM teams, are the least thought of part of the military. We get the least respect in peacetime and then have to pull miracles in war to keep the skies clear and our armed forces safe. You'll, overtime, come to realise that your superiors are often uninformed about the correct way to use SAM systems. In Dhornaper, the generals keep out of our way and let us at the brigade level handle stuff ourselves. Your military may be different...

...

Contrary to official Dhora doctrine, none of our SAM teams fire from the maximum range of the SAM systems for two reasons:

[List=1]
[*]From maximum range, the enemy has the easiest chance of escaping your engagement envelope. You want to hug their belt as much as possible, fire from sub-20km ranges to deny them escape.
[*]From maximum range, you must illuminate the enemy much longer with your fire control radar. The longer you illuminate, the more likely you are to be hit with an anti-radiation missile. Keep all radar emissions to under 20 seconds. Radiating for less than 20 seconds will prevent an anti-radiation missile from being able to exactly determine your location, increasing the chances that it will miss your equipment.
[/list]

...

After every illumination and missile launch, you must relocate to a new location. Treat your old location as compromised.

...

Always illuminate with your radar imitators at the same time to reduce the likelihood of being hit with an anti-radiation missile. Imitators are cheap and expendable.

...

Camouflage your equipment and create decoys so optical observers cannot see your real equipment, and hit your decoy equipment. We have supplied you with inflatable decoys, use them wisely.

...

After every engagement, report to command with the details of what happened, how, and why. Your reports will help train your comrades from your experience.

...

You must maintain three levels of readiness:

[List=1]
[*]Readiness Level 1 is when your team is at their stations and ready to engage immediately.
[*]Readiness Level 2 is when your team is at their stations but the equipment is off. Still, your team should be able to switch to Readiness Level 1 at a moments notice.
[*]Readiness Level 3 is when your team is ready to enter Readiness Level 1 within ten minutes. You do not have to be at your stations for this.
[/list]

Any readiness worse than Readiness Level 3 is unacceptable.

...

Your P-18 is an early warning radar. It can detect aircraft at up to 360km in ideal circumstances. Circumstances are, of course, never ideal. It is too inaccurate to guide your missiles. Since it uses an extremely long wavelength, it will not be detected by the enemy, nor will it be targeted by anti-radiation missiles. Still, usage should be minimal to lower maintenance requirements.

When an enemy aircraft is detected on the P-18, it will appear as a round circle. You will get approximate direction and range for it. You then must use your Pantsir acquisition radar to get the altitude of the targe and the exact range and direction from which you can fire your missiles. Remember, never use the acquisition radar for more than 20 seconds and never at ranges longer than 20km.

...

Stealth technology is not invisible. Your P-18 will detect stealth aircraft at ranges of up to 100km. Your Pantsir acquisition radar will acquire them at closer than 20km just fine.

...

Towed decoys can fool your teams. Over time, you will become experienced enough to notice decoys. A key giveaway is that your radar will see two targets at the same altitude and going in the same direction. The fainter one is typically the real aircraft. The one that appears to be trailing the other is always the decoy. You will learn to distinguish them in time.

...

Jammers are a unique threat. They will prevent your acquisition radar from working. The Pantsirs have a counter to this: it is called passive angle tracking. Simply, it can use multiple Pantsirs to triangulate the location of the jammer without needing to turn the radar on. With the location triangulated, you can fire a missile and destroy the jamming aircraft. Of course, the best counter to a jamming aircraft is using your own aircraft and firing air-to-air anti-radiation missiles. Using the Pantsirs for this is a last resort if your air force is too battered to fulfill this task.

...

Always fire two missiles at each target. Each one no more than three seconds apart  This will maximise the chances of a hit. Any more than two is wasteful and increases the time you need to keep your target illuminated with the acquisition radar.

...

Any questions?"[/spoiler][/quote]

[b][u]Training Continued[/u][/b]

The colonel waits and, as there were no more questions, he proceeds.

"I will now play two training tapes for you. These will show live firing exercises and operational use of the Pantsir and P-18 radars in conjunction. Watch these tapes carefully."

With that, he steps to the side and orders the technicians to play the tapes on the projector.

[Spoiler=Video Tape 1]
The first video begins with an aerial overview of the SAM battalion at night time, the traditional time that most air sorties are carried out due to low visibility with the naked eye and with cameras. In the center of the mock up battalion position is a Pantsir. Less than a hundred metres away is the P-18-2 early warning radar alongside a mobile power station. Nearby, also less than a hundred metres away, is the maintenance vehicles. all of the vehicles are camouflaged under trees and with twigs, branches, and shrubbery surrounding them. At half a kilometres away, in three different directions from the Pantsir, are three battery powered radar imitators. The enlisted men entrusted with the radar imitators are hiding behind trees and in ditches. The radar imitators are connected to the Pantsir by lengthy cables.

Switching scenes, the video now places the observer inside the Pantsir. It shows two officers: the battalion commanding officer and the missile guidance officer.

The commanding officer observes his screen, displaying the P-18 radar data, as he sees three targets approach from 60km towards him. several sweeps go by, the target is now 17-18km away and only one is approaching. The other two turned back. A few more sweeps go by, the target is at 14-15km, well within the engagement envelope.

The commanding officer shouts to the missiles guidance officer: "Azimuth 210 14km search!"

The missile guidance officer turns the radar towards azimuth 210 and flicks the switch from "equivalent" to "antenna", turning the radar on.

The missile guidance officer relays this to the commander: "Antenna!"

Less than a second later, the radar turns on. The scene quickly switches to the radar imitators, all of them turn to aiming at the same place, each one activating as follows: two before the Pantsir's radar is on at staggered intervals, and one after the Pantsir's radar is on. This is to sow confusion about the real radar and reduce the chance of the Pantsir being hit by an anti-radiation missile.

The scene changes again, the missile guidance officer frantically guides the radar to search around azimuth 210 with the keyboard. Three seconds go by and the target was not acquired.

The commanding officer shouts "Stop search, equivalent!"

The missile guidance officer quickly switches the radar to "equivalent", meaning that the radar is off but the radar can still be rotated and adjusted before being switched to "antenna", which means on and emitting.

"Equivalent!"

A few seconds go by and the commander again shouts his order: "Azimuth 230 search!"

The missile guidance officer again steers the radar before turning it on.

"Antenna!"

A few seconds go by. The commanding officer was again about to order a halt but the missile guidance officer has the target: "Tracking manually!"

The video shows the radar screen, a thin narrow target appears on the Pantsir's radar.

A few seconds go by again.

"Station tracking target, target in approach, distance 13 altitude 6 velocity 700 velocity!"

The commander understood the information. The target is 13km away, at 6km altitude, and 700km/h velocity. The probability of intercept was high.

"Launch!"

The missile guidance officer fires the first missile.

"First missile launched, first missile tracking!"

Three seconds later he launches the second missile.

"Second missile launched, second missile tracking!"

The missiles fly through the air, the target has no escape now. Ten seconds later, the missile guidance officer, who was manually tracking the target with the radar reports back.

"First missile hit!"

The video again shows the radar screen: a circle expands over the target and contracts, meaning he missile has exploded and hit the target.

Seconds later: "Second missile hit, target destroyed, distance 12 altitude 8!"

The commanding officer orders back: "Stop radar!"

"Equivalent!"

The engagement was over. From first emission to radar off was just 23 seconds, slightly above the prescribed maximum.

The commanding officer bellows over his radio: "Evacuate to reserve position."

In five minutes, the Pantsir is disconnected from the radar imitators and has moved out. Five minutes after and the radar imitators and cables connecting them to the pantsir have been spooled up and are ready to be transported by the brigades logistics to the reserve position. Five minutes after, the P-18 is packed up, the mobile power station is packed up, and everything, including the maintenance vehicles, have evacuated.

The whole positions is cleared and the battalion on the move in 15 minutes. The target they hit was a stealth bomber.
[/spoiler]

[spoiler=Video Tape 2]
The second tape is noticeably shorter. Having already acquainted the viewers with a SAM battalion's setup and basic operation, it begins in the Pantsir immediately.

The commanding officer's display shows 6-8 planes at over 100km away. After several sweeps of the P-18, one of the targets appears at 30km away and is flying towards them. Other targets, in pairs, are flying at different angles towards different locations. Classic SEAD tactics. Trying to provoke a radar emission from SAM systems. The commanding officer focuses on the target at 30km away.

"Azimuth 310 preparation!"

"Prepared!"

A few sweeps go by, the target is at 17km.

"17km search!"

"Antenna!"

The missile guidance officer immediately finds the target but pauses slightly as he notices two targets. One slightly to the right of the one he is tracking with a fainter signature. Seeing that both are at the same altitude and on the same path, he quickly deduces which one is the towed decoy and switches to tracking the fainter target.

"Tracking manually!"

And immediately after: "Station tracking target..."

The commanding officer doesn't wait to hear the parameters; he recognises that if the target was acquired so quickly, the probability of intercept is high. He immediately orders a launch.

"Launch!"

"First missile launched, first missile tracking! ... Second missile launched, second missile tracking!"

Less than ten seconds later, the missile hits.

"First missile hit! ... Second missile hit, target destroyed, distance 14 altitude 10!"

"Stop radar!"

"Equivalent!"

The engagement was over in 15 seconds. The target they hit was a non-stealth fighter aircraft.

The video tape shows one of the radar imitators nearby, damaged by an anti-radiation missile.
[/spoiler]

[spoiler= The Establishment of the Karwin Autonomous Republic
[sub]An Expansion Post[/sub]] 

The morning of 10 December was cold, dark, and wet. The island of Tel Karwin was still sleeping on this Sunday morning, but behind the scenes, heated negotiations were taking place between the Government of Ostarev and the Regional Government of Tel Karwin. These negotiations are centered on the rights of the people on the island, their freedom of religion, and their ability to retain the rights to their oil.

Following the collapse of the Republic of Tallisland, the people of Tel Karwin have been left to fend for themselves. The people, a religious minority in the area, have turned to the Government of Ostarev to see if they can establish a deal for their security. The negotiations about this security, however, have been tough. The Ostarevi Government wants to incorporate the area as part of the Republic. But the people of Tel Karwin wish to retain their autonomy, their freedom of religion, and the rights to their vast oil deposits.

Through many weeks of debate, these issues have been tossed around and mulled over, and today an agreement may finally be reached. The current agreement hinges on the recognition of Tel Karwin as the Karwin Autonomous Republic. This recognition is important, as it will give the area a vast amount of autonomy. They will be able to create their own constitution, establish their own legislature, a local police force, and a local national guard. The area will still be beholden to the Constitution of Ostarev and to the President of Ostarev. However, they will have special recourse for issues that affect them.

Next, the religious freedom of all individuals who live in the territory will be respected and upheld. This is a core tenet of the Ostarevi Constitution. The Karwin Autonomous Zone will also have the ability to appeal to the Ostarev Constitutional Court at any time if they believe any of their rights are being violated. The Ostarevi Constitutional Court will also accept the Karwin Constitution as a document of equal weight to the Ostarevi Constitution.

Finally, Karwin will waive all rights to its oil deposits. This allows Ostarevi oil companies to move into the region and begin extraction as soon as the deal is finalized. This is in response to the Ostarevi Government granting Karwin the level of autonomy it is receiving, the ability to form a local national guard, and the recognition of its constitution as having equal weight to the Ostarevi Constitution. The Government of Karwin will also receive an annual payment from the Ostarevi Government for the right to extract and refine oil from all mainland Karwin oil fields.

This deal was not what Karwini leadership was hoping for, but they realized that it was probably the best they were going to get. By that afternoon, they had approved it in the Karwini Legislature, and it took effect early on the morning of 17 December. By that point, Ostarevi troops were already on the island and beginning to cohabitate with local security forces. A language barrier did make communication difficult, but not impossible. Over the next few weeks, the Ostarevi Armed Forces would focus on teaching the National Guardsmen to speak Belorevi. These soldiers would be the founding members of the Karwin National Guard. Ostarevi commanders would also assist in training the new National Guardsmen.

Ostarevi companies would swarm onto the island, buying up plots of land, commercial property for sale, and more. These businesses would look to capitalize on the new market before their competitors could. This was especially prevalent in the extraction of offshore oil. These companies would buy up all the land they could get their hands on and immediately begin the process of acquiring permits for offshore oil extraction.

The Ostarevi Government would pass laws requiring the teaching of Belorevi in Karwini schools, allowing Karwin to set its own history education standards, and allowing Karwin to set the protocols for emergency management on the island. These laws were seen as a gesture of goodwill from the Ostarevi Government. Although most Karwini leadership considered these privileges they already had, so the gesture fell flat to some. But both parties do hope that this is an agreement that will last well into the future. 

-

The Ostarevi authorities are also reorganizing the Toqabileh regions under the control of the Republic of Ostarev. These regions have been problematic for the Ostarevi Government for quite some time, plagued by persistent unrest and a long history of strained relations with the central government. The Toqabileh region is home to the Toqastani people, a distinct ethnic and cultural group with deep historical ties to the land and a strong tradition of local self-rule.

For decades, the Toqastani population has openly resisted Ostarevi authority. Many Toqastani communities openly support resistance movements opposed to the Ostarevi Government, providing recruits, shelter, and logistical support to insurgent groups operating in the region. Public demonstrations are common, and protests frequently erupt in response to new laws, regulations, or security measures imposed by Ostarev. These demonstrations often escalate into clashes with security forces, further deepening resentment on both sides.

Ostarevi officials argue that the reorganization of the Toqabileh regions is necessary to restore stability, improve governance, and integrate the region more fully into the Republic. Critics, both within Toqabileh and abroad, view the effort as an attempt to dilute Toqastani autonomy and weaken resistance through administrative restructuring and increased security presence. As the reorganization proceeds, tensions remain high, and many fear that the changes may inflame the very unrest Ostarev claims it is trying to resolve.

[/spoiler]

[spoiler= The Island of Velkari
[sub]An Expansion Post[/sub]]

The Island of Velkari is one of the most beautiful places you can find in the Belorevi nations. The island is known for its temperate climate and sunny beaches. It is a vacation spot for many of the wealthiest people in Kyratov and Ostarev. The island sits far away from the troubles that are usually present on the mainland of the Belorevi region, and its people benefit from that. 

The island was once home to the largest naval base in the Belorevan Union of Socialist Republics, but after its fall, its significance has waned. The island now mostly focuses on tourism and a vast fishing industry, which drives most of the food production on the island. This beautiful island has many lots for sale for the rich and wealthy all over the world, and with favorable tax rates, maybe you too can call it a lovely summer home in Shamat. 

The island has many great amenities including sporting events, the aforementioned lovely beaches, and plenty of recreational activities. You can also visit one of the many historical sights on the island. The island is home to many species of animals that cannot be found anywhere else in the world. Make your next vacation a bucket list stop, and come to Velkari. 

[/spoiler]
